newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees rising deaths, injuries from landmines.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees rising deaths, injuries from landmines.

text.p: U.S. Federal health officials said on Thursday that 9,600 people are killed by land mines worldwide every year and another 14,400 are wounded, double the number of injuries logged in 1980.

"We really want to increase awareness about the public health impact of landmines among the medical and public health community," said Michael Qualls, a public health adviser in the Center for Disease Control's International Emergency and Refugee Health Program.
The International Committee of the Red Cross estimates that about 120 million land mines are buried in 71 countries throughout the world and another 2 million to 5 million are planted every year.
Officials say that a person is killed or maimed by a land mine every 20 minutes somewhere in the world.

This devastating toll has sparked an international campaign to rid the world of land mines. Britain's Princess Diana has made the issue her personal crusade, this week visiting Bosnia to highlight the dangers of the devices.

A U.N.-sponsored conference in Geneva in May, 1996, agreed to limit the use of some land mines but stopped short of a ban because some countries argue they should remain a legitimate form of military defense. Ninety-five countries -- but not the United States -- have agreed to sign a ban on land mines.
The CDC noted that while mines are relatively inexpensive to produce, ranging in cost from $3 to $30, clearing a single mine can cost $300 to $1,000.

Treating a land mine survivor costs an average of $3,000 to $5,000, but the figure can be much higher, the CDC said. In one case, it cost $1 million to treat an American Refugee Committee nursing coordinator after her vehicle struck a land mine in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Both of her legs were amputated below the knee and she required extensive facial reconstruction surgery.
One-third of surviving land mine victims require amputation, a procedure which requires almost three times as much blood as other war-related injuries.
Many of the countries with land mines require help from the international community because they do not have the resources to clear the mines or treat those who are injured by them, the CDC said.
Qualls said health-care and relief workers are often the victims of land mines as they are called in to help victims of regional conflicts.

"By nature of the work that we do in our international emergency response and refugee health activities here, a lot of times we are basically in the field where land mines are a threat to us and our colleagues in the international agencies we routinely collaborate with," he said.
The International Committee of the Red Cross estimates that some countries, such as Afghanistan, Angola and Cambodia, each have about 10 million mines.
